hints: Recall the general decomposition for a Group 2 carbonate, $\text{MCO}_{3} \rightarrow \text{MO} + \text{CO}_{2}$, and think about what physical state the metal oxide product will be in.
walkthrough:
Picture what decomposition does**
Think of a carbonate as a metal oxide with a $\text{CO}_{2}$ molecule locked inside it, $\text{MCO}_{3}$. On strong heating that $\text{CO}_{2}$ is driven off as a colourless gas, so $\text{CuCO}_{3} \rightarrow \text{CuO} + \text{CO}_{2}$. The oxide is a solid, so you never get a completely empty tube.

Link to the copper colour**
You know copper(II) oxide is a black solid. So when green anhydrous $\text{CuCO}_{3}$ is heated strongly, you see the gas escape and a black solid residue of $\text{CuO}$ left behind.
Final answer: A black solid remains ($\text{CuO}$ formed with evolution of $\text{CO}_{2}$).

hints: Start by stating the observed trend in how easily $\text{MgCO}_{3}$ to $\text{BaCO}_{3}$ decompose on heating down Group 2.
Compare the $\text{M}^{2+}$ ions down the group in terms of ionic radius while the charge stays as $2+$.
Think about how a small, highly charging cation distorts the electron cloud of the large $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ ion and why that helps it break into $\text{O}^{2-}$ and $\text{CO}_{2}$.
walkthrough:
State the trend clearly**
Going down Group 2 from magnesium to barium, the carbonates become harder to decompose. $\text{MgCO}_{3}$ decomposes easily on gentle heating, while $\text{BaCO}_{3}$ needs very strong heating. In other words, thermal stability increases down the group.

Track the cation size**
All the ions are $\text{M}^{2+}$, so the charge is identical. What changes is size. $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is very small, $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is much larger. A small ion packs the same $2+$ charge into a tiny volume, so it has a very high charge density and is strongly polarising. A large ion has a low charge density and is only weakly polarising.

See what polarisation does to carbonate**
Picture the $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ ion next to $\text{M}^{2+}$. A small $\text{M}^{2+}$ pulls hard on the electrons in the C-O bonds, distorting the carbonate electron cloud toward itself. This weakens the C-O bonds and makes it easy for the ion to split: $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-} \rightarrow \text{O}^{2-} + \text{CO}_{2}$. That $\text{O}^{2-}$ then joins the $\text{M}^{2+}$ to give $\text{MO}$.

Join trend to explanation**
Down the group, larger $\text{M}^{2+}$ distorts $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ less, the C-O bonds stay stronger, more heat is needed to break them, so stability increases. This is why polarising power, which falls as ionic radius rises, controls thermal stability.

Final answer: Thermal stability increases down Group 2.
Down the group the radius of $\text{M}^{2+}$ increases, so charge density decreases.
Polarisation / distortion of the $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ ion by $\text{M}^{2+}$ decreases, so decomposition to oxide and $\text{CO}_{2}$ is less favoured.

hints: Count the total valence electrons to place: C brings 4, each N brings 5, plus 2 for the $2-$ charge, and decide how many shared pairs are needed to give every atom an octet.
Recall the key requires $\bullet$ for C electrons, $\times$ for N electrons and $\Box$ for the two added ions electrons, and that the whole unit must sit inside square brackets with $2-$.
walkthrough:
Count electrons first**
Do not guess. Carbon is Group 14 so $4$ valence electrons ($\bullet$). Each nitrogen is Group 15 so $5$ valence electrons ($\times$), giving $10$ in total. Add $2$ more ($\Box$) for the $2-$ charge. Total $= 4 + 10 + 2 = 16$ electrons, which is $8$ pairs.

Work out the bonding**
Arrange as $\text{N}$ $\text{C}$ $\text{N}$. To give carbon an octet with only single bonds would leave nitrogens short, so carbon forms a double bond to each nitrogen, $\text{N}=\text{C}=\text{N}$. Each double bond uses $4$ electrons, so $8$ electrons are shared in the two overlap circles, using $4$ pairs.

Place the lone pairs**
You have $8$ pairs total and have used $4$ in bonding, so $4$ pairs remain as lone pairs. Carbon already has an octet from the two double bonds, so all remaining pairs go on the nitrogens, two lone pairs on each N. Make sure the two $\Box$ electrons appear as part of these lone pairs, and keep $\bullet$ and $\times$ correctly labelled.

Finish the ion presentation**
Enclose the whole $\text{N}$ $\text{C}$ $\text{N}$ diagram in square brackets with $2-$ outside at the top right, to show it is the discrete $\text{CN}_{2}^{2-}$ ion.

Final answer: Linear $\text{N}=\text{C}=\text{N}$ unit with two $\text{C}=\text{N}$ double bonds shown as shared $\bullet$ / $\times$ pairs in the overlap regions, two lone pairs on each N atom (including the $\Box$ electrons), all enclosed in square brackets with $2-$ charge.

hints: The only calcium containing white insoluble solid that can form from $\text{Ca}^{2+}$, C, O from water, is the common carbonate, think which anion uses C and O.
Write the skeleton $\text{CaCN}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow$ calcium solid $+ \text{NH}_{3}$ and balance N then H then O to find how many waters are needed.
walkthrough:
Deduce the white solid**
You are told the products are an insoluble white solid plus ammonia only. All the nitrogen from $\text{CaCN}_{2}$ must go to $2\text{NH}_{3}$. That leaves Ca, C and O from water to make the solid. The familiar insoluble white calcium salt containing carbon and oxygen is calcium carbonate, $\text{CaCO}_{3}$.

Balance the equation**
Start with N: one $\text{CaCN}_{2}$ contains $2$ N, so you need $2\text{NH}_{3}$:
$$\text{CaCN}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CaCO}_{3} + 2\text{NH}_{3}$$
Now H: right side has $6$ H, so need $3\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. Check O: $3$ O on left, $3$ O in $\text{CaCO}_{3}$ on right. Ca and C already balance at $1$ each. The finished balanced equation is:
$$\text{CaCN}_{2} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CaCO}_{3} + 2\text{NH}_{3}$$
